title: Building Burrow
rules: Standard library only in everything that builds: tool directives (M.1) may require modules that never reach any package's import graph, and the single real exception is Q.4 (marked sdk: true, in its own module).
Each level produces exactly one part; parts are consumed by later levels (see check_graph.py).
Go 1.24 minimum. Time-based suites use an injectable clock (store.WithClock + testkit.FakeClock), never testing/synctest.

chapters.name: Boot Sector
chapters.line: Toolchain, modules and the test loop every level uses.

levels.title: Power On
levels.brief: Create the burrow module and a burrowd binary with a testable run() function, proper exit codes and usage text.
levels.idea: A program whose whole behaviour lives in a testable run() function
build: `go mod init burrow` with `go 1.24` in go.mod (done for you)
`version`, `help` and usage errors with the right exit codes and streams
`gofmt` and `go vet ./...` clean, from this level on
levels.win: `burrowd version` prints `burrowd 0.1.0` and exits 0; usage mistakes exit 2 with usage on stderr; the built binary behaves the same; gofmt and go vet are clean.
hints: Keep main to one line. Everything else lives in run, which tests call directly with buffers for stdout and stderr.
A `switch args[0]` with `case "version", "-version", "--version":` handles a command and its flag spellings together.
Write usage once as a const and `fmt.Fprint(w, usage)` it to whichever writer the case calls for.
levels.wild: spf13/cobra and urfave/cli generate this shape; the run(args, stdout, stderr) pattern is what makes any CLI testable

levels.title: Test Bench
levels.brief: Write the one key validator every engine and protocol will use, and learn Go's testing loop and error wrapping on the way.
levels.idea: Table-driven tests and error wrapping
build: Your own table-driven tests in `store/` (`store/validate_test.go` is a good name), using `t.Run` subtests and `errors.Is`; they are graded by mutation, see below
An `ExampleValidateKey` with a `// Output:` comment, so `go doc` shows a worked example and `go test` checks it
levels.win: 8 valid and 17 invalid keys classified correctly, errors wrap ErrInvalidKey, quote the key, and stay short for huge keys; your own tests catch all five planted bugs and your example runs.
go: for range over strings (runes vs bytes)
mutation testing (why a test must be able to fail)
hints: len(s) counts bytes, which is what the limit is in. utf8.ValidString checks encoding.
`for _, r := range key` walks runes. Check unicode.IsSpace(r) || unicode.IsControl(r).

For long keys quote only a prefix: fmt.Errorf("%w: %q... is %d bytes", ErrInvalidKey, key[:20], len(key)). For your own tests, one table row per rule in the spec (250 vs 251 bytes, a tab, bad UTF-8, 126 two-byte runes) is exactly what the mutants are planted against.
levels.wild: go test and the testing package are the whole story; testify and go-cmp are common add-ons, neither is needed

chapters.name: Memory
chapters.line: The store contract and its first engine: correct, concurrent, versioned, expiring.

levels.title: Register File
levels.brief: The store contract and its first engine: an in-memory map that gets missing keys, empty values and shared memory right.
levels.idea: A map behind a small interface, with copy semantics for everything that crosses the boundary
build: Copy byte slices in and out; return fresh slices from Keys
levels.win: Missing keys return ErrNotFound, empty values exist, no aliasing either way, cancelled contexts change nothing, Keys is sorted, and the storetest.Run conformance suite passes.
hints: Writing to a nil map panics. Make the map in NewMemory.
Slices share backing arrays. bytes.Clone(v) makes an independent copy; note bytes.Clone(nil) is nil, so decide what Get returns for an empty value.
Check ctx.Err() and ValidateKey at the top of each method, before touching the map. Keys: collect matches with strings.HasPrefix, then slices.Sort.
levels.wild: This is the shape of every Go repository interface; the Store interface here is etcd's clientv3.KV with fewer options

levels.title: Arbiter
levels.brief: Make the store safe for many goroutines at once, and meet the race detector.
levels.idea: Data races, the race detector, and one way to win: a mutex around the shared state
build: Make every Memory method safe under concurrent use
Try removing the protection and watch the race detector catch you
levels.win: Race-free under the hammer: disjoint writers, a mixed Set/Get/Delete/Keys hammer over 32 hot keys, and Len/Keys during writes, with no torn values.
go: channels as an alternative to locks
hints: A zero-value sync.RWMutex is ready to use; never copy a struct that contains one. Lock inside methods so callers can't forget.
RLock for Get/Keys/Len, Lock for Set/Delete. Hold the lock for as little as possible, but for the whole check-then-act.

If you'd rather have one goroutine own the map and serve requests from a channel, that passes too; Raft (10.1) will require that pattern. Keep the mutex version for now if you want the idiomatic Go answer first.
levels.wild: go test -race (ThreadSanitizer); sync.Map exists for a narrow case (append-only caches) and is not what you want here

levels.title: Versions
levels.brief: A version per key and compare-and-swap: the primitive behind locks, counters and ETags.
levels.idea: Optimistic concurrency: a version per key and compare-and-swap
build: `Entry.Version`, maintained by Set, CAS and Delete
`CompareAndSwap` and `CompareAndDelete`, atomic under the Arbiter's lock
levels.win: Versions count as specified, mismatches change nothing, and 50 goroutines doing 200 CAS-retry increments each land on exactly 10,000 with at least one retry observed.
hints: Store a small struct per key: value and version. Version lives with the value, not in a second map.
CAS is Get-then-Set under one write lock. The only new logic is the comparison in between.

Write the counter loop in a test helper first: `for { e, _ := Get; n := parse(e.Value); if _, err := CAS(key, e.Version, n+1); err == nil { break } }`. That loop is what 8.1's lock and 11.3's checker are made of.
levels.wild: etcd Txn with mod_revision compares, memcached cas tokens, HTTP ETag/If-Match, DynamoDB condition expressions

levels.title: Decay
levels.brief: Keys that expire, decided lazily at read time on an injectable clock, plus the atomic CAS-with-TTL a lease needs.
levels.idea: Lazy expiry: don't delete on a timer, decide at read time
build: An expiry check on every read and write path, under the lock, using one clock reading per operation
`Set` and `CompareAndSwap` clear the TTL; CAS treats expired as absent
levels.win: Expiry is exact to the nanosecond on the fake clock, expired keys are invisible on every path, CompareAndSwapWithTTL creates with an expiry atomically, Touch extends, Set clears, and storetest.RunTTL passes.
hints: Store expireAt per entry (zero = never). Read the clock once at the top of each method into now, and write one unexported alive(e, now) bool used on every path.
WithClock is the first functional option: `type Option func(*options)`, an unexported options struct with now func() time.Time defaulting to time.Now, and NewMemory applying each opt.
Expired entries can stay in the map for now; 1.5 cleans them up. The only rule is that nobody can observe them.
levels.wild: Redis EXPIRE/PERSIST/TTL and its lazy expiry on access; etcd leases; memcached's lazy expiration

levels.title: Janitor
levels.brief: A background sweeper you can stop cleanly, with an exactly-once eviction hook.
levels.idea: A background goroutine with a lifecycle: start, do work on a ticker, stop, and prove it stopped
build: A sweeper goroutine on a time.Ticker that removes entries the injected clock says are expired
`Close()` that stops it and waits, idempotent, via sync.Once and a done channel
levels.win: The sweeper evicts 100 expired keys with no reads, OnEvict fires exactly once per key even with racing readers and may call back into the store, and no goroutine is left after Close.
hints: Sweep: lock, walk the map, collect expired entries into a slice, delete them, unlock, then call OnEvict for each. Callbacks never run under the lock.
Exactly-once: whoever removes the entry under the write lock owns the OnEvict call. A reader that notices expiry must take the write lock and re-check before removing; the sweeper may have beaten it.
Close: `once.Do(func(){ close(stop) })`, then `<-done`, which the sweeper closes on exit. The sweeper selects on the ticker and stop.
levels.wild: Redis's active expire cycle; patrickmn/go-cache's janitor; every Go server you'll write has a goroutine that needs exactly this Close discipline

chapters.name: Codec
chapters.line: Bytes with a length in front. The one codec the wire, the log, the RPC layer and the queues all share.

levels.title: Record
levels.brief: Length-prefixed records over any reader and writer: the one codec the wire, the log, RPC and the queues share.
levels.idea: Length-prefixed framing over any io.Reader/io.Writer, with exact EOF rules and limits checked before allocating
build: A fuzz target of your own in `wire/` (name it `FuzzRecord` or similar, not `FuzzL…`) with a seed corpus, that ReadRecord and the round trip never panic on
levels.win: Golden bytes match, round trips survive one-byte readers, EOF rules are exact, a 4 GiB length doesn't allocate, Write is called once per record, and the fuzzer finds nothing; your own fuzz target survives two seconds of fuzzing.
hints: conn.Read can return fewer bytes than asked. io.ReadFull loops for you and turns a mid-read EOF into io.ErrUnexpectedEOF.
Read the 4-byte header into a stack array; if it returns io.EOF with zero bytes that's the clean EOF, anything else is unexpected. Check the length before make().
Build the whole record with binary.BigEndian.AppendUint32 then append the payload, write it once, and compare n to len(buf).
levels.wild: protobuf length-delimited streams, gRPC's 5-byte message frame, Kafka record batches, Redis RESP bulk strings: every binary protocol has this part

levels.title: Frame
levels.brief: The KV message laid out inside a record; the record's length means the value needs none of its own.
levels.idea: A typed message laid out inside a record; the record's length means the last field needs none of its own
build: `EncodeFrame`/`DecodeFrame` with the exact layout and limits
levels.win: Golden bytes match, every field round-trips, unknown ops and oversized keys and values are rejected both ways without allocating, and the fuzzer finds nothing.
hints: Encode into one slice with binary.BigEndian.AppendUint64 and friends; the value is just appended last.
Decode: check len(p) >= 19 first, then the key length against both MaxKeySize and the remaining bytes, then slice. Copy the value out of p.
Write a `var opNames = map[Op]string` and use it for String(); IsRequest is `o < 0x80`.
levels.wild: Redis RESP3 and the memcached binary protocol are this with more ops; gRPC puts the typed message in protobuf inside the same kind of frame

chapters.name: Wire
chapters.line: Raw TCP, a frame server, a client that is itself a Store, deadlines, and clean shutdown.

levels.title: Loopback
levels.brief: Your first network server: an accept loop you will reuse, and an echo server on top of it.
levels.idea: Accept in a loop, one goroutine per connection, and a clean exit when the listener closes
build: `ServeConns` with goroutine per connection and the net.ErrClosed rule
`ServeEcho` on top of it with `io.Copy(conn, conn)` and `defer conn.Close()`
Two slog lines per connection with `remote` and `bytes` attributes
levels.win: Echoes 50 concurrent clients and a 4 MiB payload, handles half-close, logs both lines, and returns nil when the listener closes.
hints: Accept blocks. `go handle(conn)` or the second client waits forever.
After ln.Close(), Accept returns an error matching errors.Is(err, net.ErrClosed). That's your clean exit.
io.Copy returns the byte count you need for the bytes attribute. slog.New(slog.DiscardHandler) stands in for a nil logger.
levels.wild: net/http's Server.Serve is this loop with timeouts and a connection state machine on top; you'll read it in H.3

levels.title: Switchboard
levels.brief: A request/reply server speaking frames from any Store, with one reply for every outcome.
levels.idea: A request/reply loop: decode a frame, call the store, map each outcome to exactly one reply
build: A per-connection loop: ReadFrame, dispatch, WriteFrame
The reply table above, including error mapping with errors.Is
A deferred `recover` in the connection goroutine, so a panicking store call costs one connection, not the process
levels.win: Every row of the reply table matches, 100 pipelined requests in one write get 100 replies in order, 40 concurrent clients see their own replies, and bad input closes only when the stream is untrustworthy; a store that panics takes down one connection and nothing else.
go: mapping errors to replies with errors.Is
interfaces as injection points (a fake Store in tests)
min and max for TTL rounding
hints: One function `handle(req Frame) (Frame, bool)` returning the reply and whether to keep the connection makes the table testable without a socket.
Map errors in one place: errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound) -> OpNotFound, store.ErrVersionMismatch -> OpMismatch, anything else -> OpError with err.Error().
Wrap conn in a bufio.Writer and Flush after each reply; wrap reads in a bufio.Reader so pipelined frames don't cost a syscall each.
levels.wild: A Redis server's command dispatch; net/rpc's server loop

levels.title: Remote Store
levels.brief: A client package whose type is itself a Store, so the conformance suite runs over TCP, plus burrowctl.
levels.idea: A client package whose type satisfies the same Store interface as the engine it talks to
build: `client.Dial` and one method per Store operation, mapping reply ops back to the store's sentinel errors
A mutex per call so 50 goroutines can share one Client
levels.win: storetest.Run, RunCAS and RunTTL pass against a Client talking to a wire.Server over loopback; 50 goroutines sharing one client never get each other's replies; burrowctl round-trips every command.
hints: One unexported `call(ctx, req Frame) (Frame, error)` does lock, WriteFrame, ReadFrame, unlock. Every public method is a thin wrapper that builds the request and interprets the reply.
Map replies in one switch: OpNotFound -> store.ErrNotFound, OpMismatch -> store.ErrVersionMismatch, OpError -> &ServerError{Msg: string(f.Value)}.
Point storetest at a factory that starts a wire.Server on testkit.Listen and dials it. If the suite passes, your client is a Store.
levels.wild: redis-go, etcd clientv3, memcache clients: a client package whose methods mirror the server's commands and whose errors are the server's sentinels

levels.title: Deadlines
levels.brief: Make every client call obey its context: deadlines, cancels, and never reusing a connection you can't trust.
levels.idea: Making a blocking network call obey a context: deadline, cancel, and never reusing a connection you can't trust
build: Set the connection deadline from ctx.Deadline() for the duration of each call
`context.AfterFunc(ctx, ...)` to interrupt a blocked read on cancel
Discard and redial after any mid-call error; report ctx.Err() when the context caused it
levels.win: Deadlines and cancels return the context's own error promptly, a timed-out connection is never reused, the server hanging up is recovered on the next call, and burrowctl -timeout exits 1 with `timeout`.
hints: Set the conn deadline from ctx.Deadline() at the start of each call and clear it after. A deadline alone can't see a cancel.
`stop := context.AfterFunc(ctx, func(){ conn.SetDeadline(time.Unix(1, 0)) }); defer stop()` makes a cancel interrupt a blocked Read.
When a call fails, check ctx.Err() first and return it; then close the conn and set it to nil so the next call redials. The mutex you already hold keeps this safe.
levels.wild: net/http's Transport does exactly this per request; database/sql drivers and gRPC clients too. context.AfterFunc (Go 1.21) replaced a goroutine-per-call idiom

levels.title: Power Down
levels.brief: Stop on Ctrl-C without dropping requests in flight: connection tracking, Shutdown, and burrowd serve.
levels.idea: Graceful shutdown: stop accepting, let in-flight work finish, bound the wait, and wire it to a signal
build: Mark connections busy from a full request read until its reply is written
levels.win: Idle connections close at once, in-flight requests finish, the context deadline force-closes, repeated and concurrent Shutdowns return nil, nothing leaks, and the binary exits 0 on SIGINT and SIGTERM.
hints: Keep the tracker's map and busy flags under one mutex. Busy means: a full request has been read and its reply hasn't been written.
Shutdown order: close the listener, then Drain. Drain's loop: CloseIdle, check Len, sleep a few ms or return on ctx.Done().
signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) gives you a context that's cancelled on Ctrl-C; call Shutdown with context.WithTimeout(10s) when it fires.
levels.wild: net/http.Server.Shutdown tracks exactly these states (StateNew/Active/Idle); Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which is this ctx

chapters.name: Persistence
chapters.line: A write-ahead log that survives kill -9, checksummed, truncatable, compacted and batched. Independent of Wire: take it first if you like.

levels.title: Write-Ahead Log
levels.brief: Survive a crash by appending every change to a log before acknowledging it; replay it as an iterator.
levels.idea: Append then fsync then acknowledge; replay as an iterator
build: Records as an `iter.Seq2` using `wire.ReadRecord` on an `io.SectionReader` so replay doesn't move the write position
levels.win: Records come back in order after a reopen, iteration can stop early, 20 concurrent appenders never interleave, and every record acknowledged before kill -9 survives.
go: re-running the test binary as a helper process
hints: Open with os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREATE and track the write offset yourself (or use O_APPEND). Replay with io.NewSectionReader(f, 0, size) so reads never touch the write position.

An iterator is a function that takes yield: `return func(yield func([]byte, error) bool) { for { rec, err := wire.ReadRecord(r); if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { return }; if !yield(rec, err) || err != nil { return } } }`.
A mutex around Append keeps records whole. Sync after the write, before returning: that's the whole contract.
levels.wild: etcd's wal package, RocksDB's WAL, Postgres XLOG; iter.Seq2 (Go 1.23) is how new std APIs expose sequences, e.g. maps.Keys and bufio.Scanner's successor patterns

levels.title: Non-volatile Store
levels.brief: Embed the Memory engine, override the writes, and pass the same conformance suite from disk.
levels.idea: Extending a type by embedding it: override the writes, inherit the reads, pass the same conformance suite
build: `durable.Store` embedding `*store.Memory`, overriding the seven mutating methods behind per-key locks
A change-record encoding carrying version and absolute expiry, with wire.OpSet / wire.OpDelete as the op byte
levels.win: The durable store passes Run, RunConcurrent, RunCAS and RunTTL, state after a restart matches exactly including versions and expiries, rejected writes and expiries don't grow the log, and every acknowledged write survives kill -9.
hints: Embed *store.Memory and only write the methods that change state. Each one: validate, lock the key's stripe, read the current entry, compute what Memory would store, Append, then Restore (or Delete). Memory.Now gives you the clock for ExpiresAt.
Log what happened, not what was asked: a CAS that succeeded is logged as a put with the full entry it produced. Replay then needs no version or TTL logic, just Restore.

Don't log evictions. A reader can evict key k, another goroutine Sets k and logs a put, and then the eviction's delete lands after the put, so replay would delete the new value. Absolute ExpiresAt in every put makes replay correct without them.
levels.wild: Redis AOF, Bitcask, the memory+log core of LevelDB's memtable; Go's embedding is how net/http middleware and io wrappers extend types without inheritance

levels.title: Parity Bits
levels.brief: Checksum every record, repair torn tails, refuse corruption, and expose Len and Truncate.
levels.idea: Trusting bytes on disk: checksum every record, repair torn tails, refuse corruption, and expose the cut
build: CRC32 inside each record payload; verify on read
Open scans, classifies torn tail vs corruption, repairs the tail
`Len` and `Truncate(n)`, maintaining a record index (offsets) built during the scan
Your own tests in `wal/` for corruption, tail repair and Truncate, on `t.TempDir()`; graded by mutation as in 0.2
levels.win: The last record cut at every byte offset repairs cleanly, a bad middle record is ErrCorrupt with the file untouched, every single bit flip is caught, zeros never become records, and Truncate(n) leaves exactly n records that survive a reopen; your own tests catch three planted bugs in corruption handling and Truncate.
hints: Checksum rec, put the CRC in front of it, and hand the whole thing to wire.WriteRecord. On read, split, verify, then yield.

A bad record is a torn tail if it reaches the end of the file or everything after it is zeros. Otherwise it's corruption. Record each good record's end offset in a slice as you scan: that slice is your index for Len and Truncate.
Truncate(n) is os.File.Truncate(offsets[n]) plus Sync, then cut the index.
levels.wild: etcd's wal records carry a CRC; Kafka segments; SQLite's WAL frames have checksums; Raft's log truncation on AppendEntries conflict (section 5.3)

levels.title: Compaction
levels.brief: Stop the log growing forever with snapshots and atomic file swaps that survive every crash point.
levels.idea: Atomic replacement: write a temp file, fsync, rename, fsync the directory, and reason about every crash point
build: Open loads the snapshot then replays; checksum the snapshot
levels.win: The log shrinks to nothing after a snapshot, every crash point between the steps recovers to the right state, a damaged snapshot fails loudly, and snapshots taken under concurrent writes lose nothing.
hints: Rename within a directory is atomic on POSIX. To make the rename itself durable, open the directory and Sync it.
Replaying the old log on top of a newer snapshot is safe because Restore is idempotent: the same entry restored twice is the same state.

Snapshot takes the exclusive side of the lock your per-key stripes sit under (one RWMutex over all writes): hold it only while you take Memory.Snapshot() and note the log length; write the file outside it, then take it again to rename and Truncate(0).
levels.wild: Redis RDB + AOF rewrite; etcd snapshots; the write-temp-then-rename idiom in every database and in `go build`'s own output

levels.title: Overclock
levels.brief: Group commit: many concurrent appends share one fsync, measured with a benchmark and a profile.
levels.idea: Group commit: many waiters, one fsync; measured before and after
build: A writer goroutine with a request channel and per-request reply channels
Sticky sync failures; Close that drains or fails in-flight appends and stops the goroutine
A benchmark of your own in `wal/` (not `BenchmarkL…`) using `b.Loop`, run before and after, and a CPU profile you look at
levels.win: Sequential appends still sync one each, 100 goroutines x 20 appends with a 2 ms sync finish in under 2 s with at most 500 syncs, a failed sync poisons the log, Close leaves nothing hanging, and the benchmark shows the difference; Syncs() is race-free from other goroutines and your own benchmark runs.
hints: Each Append sends request{rec, done chan error} to the writer and waits on done.
Writer loop: block for one request, then drain more without blocking (select with default) up to a size limit, AppendRecord them into one buffer, write, sync once, reply to all.

Once a sync fails, remember the error and return it for every later batch without writing. Close: stop new appends first, then close the request channel (only the owner closes) and wait for the writer to exit. Count syncs with atomic.Uint64.Add in the writer and read them with Load.
levels.wild: Postgres commit_delay / group commit, InnoDB's log group commit, etcd's batched fsync; errgroup is not this, this is a classic actor loop

chapters.name: Assembly
chapters.line: Wire meets Persistence: the daemon keeps its promises across kill -9.

levels.title: Non-volatile Daemon
levels.brief: Wire meets Persistence: burrowd serve -data keeps its promises across kill -9.
levels.idea: Composing two finished subsystems into a product, and proving the composition with the real binary
build: Snapshot on shutdown and whenever durable.Store.LogLen() reaches -snapshot-every
levels.win: Set 500 keys through burrowctl, SIGKILL the daemon, restart it: every key, version and TTL is back; a clean shutdown leaves a snapshot and a tiny log.
hints: serve already has a store variable. Make it a store.Store and pick the engine from the flag; everything else is unchanged. That's what the interface bought you.
Check LogLen after each write (or on a ticker) and snapshot from a goroutine so writers aren't blocked for the whole file write; Snapshot itself pauses them only briefly.
Snapshot before Shutdown returns, after Drain, so no write races the file.
levels.wild: This is `redis-server --appendonly yes` or `etcd --data-dir`; the shape of every stateful service's main()

chapters.name: HTTP by Hand
chapters.line: An HTTP/1.1 server on raw TCP in three parts: parser, writer, router. Just enough to make net/http's gifts visible.

levels.title: Request Line
levels.brief: Speak HTTP over a raw socket: parse the request line and headers strictly.
levels.idea: Parsing a text protocol strictly: lines, tokens, limits, and the right error for each failure
build: `ReadRequest` with the RFC 9112 token rules and both size limits
A `Server` on `wire.ServeConns` that serves the hello page
levels.win: Parses everything valid, rejects 16 kinds of malformed request with ErrMalformed, enforces both limits, and serves net/http's client.
go: your own map type with methods
hints: Count bytes as you read lines and stop at MaxHeaderBytes. br.ReadSlice('\n') returns bufio.ErrBufferFull for long lines: keep appending.
strings.Split(line, " ") must give exactly three non-empty parts; a double space gives an empty one.
Header names are tokens: letters, digits and !#$%&'*+-.^_`|~. A space before the colon makes the name invalid. Write `isToken(s string) bool` once.
levels.wild: net/http's textproto.Reader and readRequest; the same rules make nginx and Envoy reject request smuggling

levels.title: Status and Body
levels.brief: Read request bodies and write real responses through a handler abstraction.
levels.idea: The handler abstraction: a ResponseWriter that buffers, a body reader that enforces a length, and a panic that becomes a 500
build: `Handler`, `HandlerFunc`, `ResponseWriter` with buffered body and header snapshot
204/304/HEAD rules, reason phrases, Date header; `recover` to 500
levels.win: net/http parses every response you write, bad lengths are 400, oversized bodies 413, truncated bodies read io.ErrUnexpectedEOF, and a panicking handler yields a 500 while the server keeps serving.
go: defer: argument evaluation time and LIFO order
hints: Buffer the body in a bytes.Buffer and write the head after the handler returns, when you know the length.
Snapshot the headers when WriteHeader is called; later changes don't count. Keep a `wroteHeader bool`.
io.LimitReader reports EOF when the underlying reader does. Wrap it in your own reader that counts and turns an early EOF into io.ErrUnexpectedEOF.
levels.wild: net/http's response and body types; the panic-to-500 behaviour you get for free from net/http is this

levels.title: Router
levels.brief: Your own router with method patterns, wildcards and specificity, and the raw KV API on it.
levels.idea: Pattern matching with specificity, methods as part of the pattern, and a resource API mounted on it
build: `Router` with pattern parsing at registration, specificity ranking and `PathValue`
`KVRoutes` with ETag on reads and writes
levels.win: Routing, percent-decoding, specificity and 405/Allow behave like Go 1.22's ServeMux, and the KV API works through a real HTTP client including 2 MiB uploads and NUL bytes.
hints: Parse patterns once at registration into segments: literal, {name}, or {name...}.
Score a match per segment (literal 2, wildcard 1, rest 0) and compare scores with slices.Compare.
Collect methods of routes whose path matched but method didn't: that's your Allow header. ETag is strconv.FormatUint(e.Version, 10) in quotes.
levels.wild: net/http.ServeMux since Go 1.22 (method patterns, wildcards, precedence); chi and gorilla/mux before that

chapters.name: net/http
chapters.line: Swap the hand-built server for net/http, speak JSON, add middleware, timeouts, a client library and an admin port.

levels.title: Front Panel
levels.brief: The same API on net/http, with ETag/If-Match turning PUT into a CAS. Chapter 6 is now the comparison.
levels.idea: The same API on net/http: handlers, ServeMux patterns, and conditional requests with ETag/If-Match
build: `http.MaxBytesReader` for 413; If-Match mapped to CompareAndSwap, If-Match + ?ttl= to CompareAndSwapWithTTL, ?ttl= alone to SetWithTTL; touch
`-http` flag in `burrowd serve`; both listeners shut down together
Your own handler tests in `api/` on `httptest.NewRecorder` or `httptest.NewServer`, graded by mutation as in 0.2 and 4.3
levels.win: The curl commands from 6.3 work unchanged, If-Match turns PUT into a CAS with 412 on mismatch, ?ttl= sets an expiry visible in Expires, and the frame port and HTTP port serve the same data; your own httptest tests catch four planted bugs.
hints: mux.HandleFunc("PUT /v1/kv/{key}", s.put). Read the key with r.PathValue("key") and validate it exactly as your router did.

levels.idea: TLS from certificates you mint yourself with crypto/x509, and what ALPN gives you
build: `burrow.Options.RootCAs` and `burrowctl -cacert`; HTTP/2 negotiated, which the tests check through `resp.Proto`
Your own test that issues a cert from a fresh CA and verifies it with `x509.Certificate.Verify`
levels.win: burrowd serves the API over https with a certificate minted by pki, curl needs --cacert and gets HTTP/2, a client without the CA is refused with an x509 error, and the frame port behaves exactly as before.
hints: Two templates: the CA with IsCA, BasicConstraintsValid and KeyUsageCertSign, signed by itself (parent == template); the leaf with DNSNames/IPAddresses, KeyUsageDigitalSignature and ExtKeyUsage, signed by the CA. x509.CreateCertificate returns DER; x509.ParseCertificate turns it back into a *Certificate for the CA struct.

tls.Certificate{Certificate: [][]byte{leafDER}, PrivateKey: key} is the in-memory form; pem.Encode with Type CERTIFICATE / PRIVATE KEY (x509.MarshalPKCS8PrivateKey) is the file form, and tls.X509KeyPair reads it back.

On the client: build the Transport yourself with TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{RootCAs: pool, MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13} and ForceAttemptHTTP2: true; without the last one a custom Transport speaks HTTP/1.1 only.
levels.wild: mkcert and step-ca do what pki does; cert-manager and Let's Encrypt's autocert (golang.org/x/crypto/acme/autocert) issue the real ones; every Go HTTPS server is http.Server.ServeTLS or a tls.Listener

levels.title: Keycard
levels.brief: Bearer tokens on the API: a token file, constant-time lookup, read and write roles, a principal in the context and the access log, and a client that sends the token.
levels.idea: Authentication as middleware, with the comparison done in constant time
build: `Auth` middleware: 401 with `WWW-Authenticate`, 403 for read tokens on writes, principal in context and in the access log
levels.win: A request without a token is 401 with WWW-Authenticate, a read token can GET but gets 403 on PUT, a write token does everything, the access log names the principal and never the token, and burrowd refuses to combine tokens with plaintext unless told to.
go: roles with iota and a principal in context
environment variables as defaults for flags
hints: Store [32]byte digests, not tokens. Lookup: hash the input once, then `match |= subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(h[:], stored[:])` across every entry, remembering the index of the match, and only decide after the loop.

Split the header with strings.Cut on the first space; strings.EqualFold(scheme, "Bearer"). Missing or bad credentials are 401 with the WWW-Authenticate header set before writeJSON; a known principal with the wrong role is 403.
r.TLS is nil on a plaintext connection, which is all the check you need. Put Auth inside AccessLog in the chain so the log line can read the principal from the context after the handler ran.
levels.wild: Every API-key scheme (Stripe, GitHub PATs) is this middleware; OAuth2 bearer tokens (RFC 6750) use the same header and the same 401/403 split; hmac.Equal and subtle.ConstantTimeCompare are what webhook verification is built on

levels.title: Handshake
levels.brief: Mutual TLS between cluster peers with per-node certificates and a membership check in the handshake, then devcluster -secure wiring the whole chapter together.
levels.idea: Identity for machines: a certificate per node, verified in both directions, with membership checked during the handshake
build: `PeerServerConfig`, `PeerClientConfig`, `AllowNames`: `ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert`, `ClientCAs`, and `VerifyConnection` (or `VerifyPeerCertificate`) for the allow check
`rpc.Server.TLS` and `rpc.DialTLS`; the 9.2 code path untouched when `TLS` is nil
`-peer-*` flags in `burrowd serve`, threaded into Raft's transport
`devcluster -secure` (with `-data <dir>` to keep the CA, certificates and tokens)
levels.win: Three nodes elect a leader and replicate over mutual TLS, a client with a certificate from another CA or with a CN that is not a peer is refused during the handshake, plaintext dials fail fast, and `devcluster -secure` brings the whole thing up with burrowctl talking to it over https with a token.
go: generating and placing secrets at startup
hints: Server side: &tls.Config{Certificates: {cert}, ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert, ClientCAs: ca.Pool(), MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13, VerifyConnection: func(cs tls.ConnectionState) error { return allow(cs.PeerCertificates[0]) }}. The chain is already verified when VerifyConnection runs.

Client side: &tls.Config{Certificates: {cert}, RootCAs: ca.Pool(), ServerName: peerID}. rpc.Server only needs `if s.TLS != nil { ln = tls.NewListener(ln, s.TLS) }` before the accept loop; DialTLS is (&tls.Dialer{Config: cfg}).DialContext.

devcluster -secure: pki.NewCA, one Issue per node with hosts {id, "localhost", "127.0.0.1"} and both ExtKeyUsages, WriteFiles into the data dir (kept with -data <dir>, as in 9.1), and the flags appended to each node's argv. Print `ca` and `token` before `cluster ready` so the tests can parse them.
levels.wild: etcd's --peer-client-cert-auth and --peer-trusted-ca-file; Consul and Nomad's auto-encrypt; SPIFFE/SPIRE issue exactly this kind of per-node identity, with the ID in a URI SAN instead of the CN; Istio does it per pod

levels.title: Redundancy

Return as soon as W succeed.

chapters.name: Queues
chapters.line: Optional. Azure Service Bus fundamentals built on your own parts: a durable queue, peek-lock as a lease, competing consumers, then the real thing in its own module.

levels.title: Mailbox
levels.brief: A durable queue broker speaking a second frame vocabulary, carrying the Service Bus message shape.
levels.idea: A durable FIFO: messages as records, sequence numbers from the log, receive-and-delete semantics
build: Message encoding (JSON body inside a Record)
WAL before ack; sequence numbers rebuilt on replay
levels.win: Send 1,000 messages, kill -9 the broker, restart: you receive all 1,000 exactly once, in order, with sequence numbers that only go up.
go: JSON struct tags and encoding rules
hints: Receive-and-delete is at-most-once; Q.2 fixes that.
The broker assigns sequence numbers; rebuild the counter from the WAL.
Keep bodies as []byte; content type tells consumers how to read them.
levels.wild: Azure Service Bus queues, SQS, RabbitMQ classic queues

levels.title: Peek-Lock
levels.brief: Receive without losing messages: lock a message while you work on it, settle it, or let it expire.
levels.idea: At-least-once delivery as a lease on a message: lock, settle, expire, redeliver, dead-letter
build: Lock state as an expiring entry
Expiry sweep redelivers and bumps DeliveryCount
levels.win: Receive and walk away: once the lock expires the message comes back with DeliveryCount 2; completing with an expired token fails with ErrLockLost; a consumer that always abandons sends its message to the DLQ after 10 deliveries. All on a FakeClock.
hints: A message is available, locked or gone. Draw the transitions first.
A lock is an entry with a TTL: SetWithTTL for lock, Touch for RenewLock, the janitor's OnEvict for expiry. You built this in chapter 1.
The DLQ is just another queue with a special name.
levels.wild: Azure Service Bus peek-lock and dead-letter queues; SQS visibility timeout

levels.title: Competing Consumers
levels.brief: Many workers drain one queue without polling and without processing anything twice.
levels.idea: Waiting without polling (sync.Cond), fairness, and prefetch as flow control
build: `ReceiveBatch(ctx, queue, max)` beside an unchanged Q.1 `Receive`
levels.win: Three consumers drain 10,000 messages: every message is completed once and each consumer handles at least 25%; with a large prefetch and slow consumers, buffered locks expire and those messages are redelivered.
go: waking a Cond on context cancel
hints: A blocked receiver wakes on Cond.Broadcast when a message arrives.
Prefetch trades latency for lock time.
Service Bus does this over AMQP with link credit.
